items.title: ChatGPT Gets Interactive Answers (Intelligent UI)
points: Paid ChatGPT users now receive answers as clickable buttons, forms, charts, and interactive tools instead of wall-of-text paragraphs.
Answers appear instantly while the model still processes complex questions, cutting search-based answer times by 44% on average.
Free users get a different model version, and OpenAI hasn't confirmed whether the new visual features are included.
The shift means ChatGPT is now making design decisions about what answers should look like, not just generating text.

items.title: AI Voice Clone Used in Virtual Kidnapping Scam
points: Scammer called a woman claiming her daughter was kidnapped by a drug cartel, then played an AI-cloned voice (synthetic audio generated to mimic a real person's voice) of her daughter crying and panicked.
Victim was kept on the phone for 5.5 hours, forced to wire money four times, and kept from calling her daughter by threats and manipulation.
The scam only collapsed when the mother called her daughter herself on a different number and found her safe at work.
The FTC warns that AI needs only a short voice clip (even from social media) to create convincing fake audio—set up a family code word now to verify emergencies.

items.title: AI Research Taste Grows Exponentially
points: P-Zero Research found top AI models' ability to choose promising experiments ('research taste') has doubled every three months since December 2025, now outperforming experienced human researchers.
Models are tested by tackling single-GPU research problems and scored on how efficiently they reach good results; neither AI nor humans produced novel methods, only tweaks of published ideas.
Giving models longer thinking time produced noticeably better choices—depth of deliberation mattered more than raw speed.

P-Zero keeps actual research tasks secret to prevent labs from training models specifically toward the benchmark (a standardized test used to compare AI systems), similar to not releasing test answers in advance.

items.title: AI Inserted Fake Quotes into Book About Truth
points: Author Steven Rosenbaum's book 'The Future of Truth' shipped with 26 fabricated or misattributed quotes that AI generated while 'improving' his writing.
A New York Times reporter exposed the problem when Rosenbaum could not source a quote from an unnamed DARPA researcher; full fact-checking revealed systemic failures.
All 26 errors survived five editing rounds and 4,000+ tracked changes—mistakes that looked natural to human readers passed through, while obvious ones got caught.
AI cannot distinguish between the author's words and quoted material, treating all text as improvable content—always verify quotes against originals before publishing AI-edited work.

items.title: Why Standard Benchmarks Don't Work
points: Published benchmarks (standardized tests comparing AI models) leak into model training data and lose validity over time; the real question is fit for your workflow, not abstract superiority.
Frontier models release every 11 days on average; meaningful verdicts emerge only after 7 days when people do actual work, not toy demos like 3D games.
Even in locked-down enterprises, choices remain: model tier selection, inference effort levels, and tool combinations all deserve testing against your real tasks.

items.title: The Five-Step Personal Benchmark System
points: Step 1—Choose 4–6 tasks mirroring your actual work balance, done regularly, trusted enough to change habits over; include at least one previous AI failure case and one where bad output is easy to spot.
Step 2—Compare current setup against 1–4 new candidates (models, harnesses, or tool combinations); baseline always included to avoid pure novelty bias.

Step 3—Run identical prompts in fresh chat sessions on each model; use manual testing, API scripts, or team platforms like LangSmith and Langfuse; run high-stakes tests multiple times since identical inputs produce different outputs; keep company data out of third-party routers.
Step 4—Blind-score anonymized outputs 1–5 with notes; side-by-side comparison beats absolute scoring; use randomization via spreadsheet, friend, or script to eliminate tool preference bias.
Step 5—Winning one test doesn't guarantee switching; weigh cost, latency, terms, features, and habit disruption against performance gains before deciding.

items.title: Actual Test Results: Seven Models Across Six Tasks
points: No single winner: Kimi K3 led on cost and speed; GPT 6.1 Sol dominated pricing negotiation at 1/10th the cost of alternatives; Opus 5.5 built the best course website; Grok 4.7 was significantly slowest.

Human and AI judge (Gemini Pro) agreed only on the pricing negotiation task; the judge scored websites from code output rather than visuals, revealing judge limitations—human blind scoring proved more reliable.

Kimi, Fable 5.1, and Opus 5 tied on LinkedIn post writing; GPT models won the course exercise; routine tasks now achievable on open-weight models (publicly downloadable AI models) without premium subscriptions.
Cost per task matters more than monthly subscription rates; $200/month plans subsidize actual token consumption, so per-use pricing wins for consumption-based users or those hitting rate limits.

items.title: Implementation Guidance
points: Match inference effort (speed/quality tradeoff) settings across models or accept OpenRouter defaults and test effort levels as a separate variable.
Operations tasks needing connectors and persistent context must run in actual harnesses (software wrappers that give a model tools and memory), not bare APIs, to reveal real-world performance.
Table-stakes work like email triage and background research: open models from Kimi, Mistral, and GLM are production-ready; explicit constraints beat vague prompts for measurable evaluation.
